title: FOMC Minutes — October 28–29, 2025
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2025-10-29 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

The Committee cut the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent. Interest on reserve balances was set at 3.90 percent and the primary credit rate at 4.0 percent. The vote was 10-2, with dissents in opposite directions: Stephen Miran wanted a half-point cut and Jeffrey Schmid wanted no change. Almost all members also agreed to end balance sheet runoff on December 1; from then, all Treasury principal will be rolled over and all agency MBS principal reinvested into Treasury bills.

Economic outlook

The federal government shutdown limited the data: government spending figures were delayed and the September jobs report was not released during the intermeeting period. Staff said growth slowed in the first half, falling in Q1 and rising strongly in Q2, and expected a boost once government operations resumed. Participants said activity was expanding at a moderate pace. Consumer spending firmed but was concentrated among higher-income households, and many highlighted strong AI and data-center investment.

Inflation

Total PCE inflation was estimated at 2.8 percent in September, up 0.5 point from a year earlier; core PCE was also 2.8 percent, unchanged from a year earlier. Participants expected inflation to stay somewhat elevated near term as tariffs pushed up core goods prices. Short-term expectations eased from their peaks, and longer-term expectations "remained well anchored."

Labor market

Job gains slowed this year and unemployment edged up but stayed low through August. The minutes did not give updated figures because of the data gap. Participants generally expected gradual softening in a low-hiring, low-layoff environment, and several flagged downside employment risks.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Money markets tightened. Repo rates rose notably relative to interest on reserves, and the gap between the effective fed funds rate and that rate was the narrowest since runoff began in 2022. Standing repo take-up occurred on several days and ON RRP usage hit its lowest average since 2021. Staff judged reserves were "moving closer to ample levels," which is why the manager recommended ending runoff soon. Over time, participants want a larger share of Treasury bills in the portfolio, a shift expected to take several years.

Risks participants flagged

  • Upside inflation risks remained elevated; tariff effects might be more persistent than expected.
  • Downside employment risks had risen and remained elevated.
  • Financial vulnerabilities judged "notable": elevated asset valuations, private-credit strains and recent bankruptcies, hedge fund leverage and stablecoin growth.
  • Possible sharp equity declines if expectations about AI were reassessed.
  • Trade tensions and limited government data.

What it signaled about next moves

Most participants saw further cuts as likely appropriate over time, but the minutes showed real division about December. Several said a December cut "could well be appropriate" if the economy evolved as expected, while many suggested holding rates for the rest of the year, and several did not see a December cut as likely. All agreed that "monetary policy was not on a preset course."

Read-through for SPY

  • A second cut plus the end of runoff added liquidity support for stocks.
  • The split over December meant a further cut was far from guaranteed, a source of near-term volatility.
  • The minutes explicitly named an AI-expectations reassessment as a risk of sharp equity declines, directly relevant to SPY's heavy tech weighting.
